_comment: Storyboard for the Grade 3 Mathematics unit lecture film, Equal Parts. Rendered by tools/create-ehel-unit-lecture.js. See lecture-video/BRIEF.md. The chapters follow the lesson's own three-part lecture (equal parts and fractions; dividing to find a fraction; comparing fractions), broken into six teaching chapters and built from the lesson page's own examples: its equal-or-not circles (one boundary shifted by half a sector, exactly as the page's shapeSvg draws a wrong one), its fifths bar coloured up to one whole, its three halves of different shapes, Zara's 12 beads, Amina's 20 shillings, 1/2 = 5/10, 2/5 + 1/5 = 3/5, 3/5 > 2/5 and 1/4 > 1/10. Every division drawn in the pictures is equal by arithmetic, never by eye.
title: Equal Parts
subtitle: Grade 3 Mathematics
objectives: Understand and explain that fractions are several equal parts of an object or shape and all the parts, taken together, equal one whole.
Understand that the relationship between the whole and the parts depends on the relative size of each, regardless of their shape or orientation.
Understand and explain that fractions can describe equal parts of a quantity or set of objects.
Understand that a fraction can be represented as a division of the numerator by the denominator (half, quarter and three-quarters).
Understand that fractions (half, quarter, three-quarters, third and tenth) can act as operators.
Recognise that two fractions can have an equivalent value (halves, quarters, fifths and tenths).
Estimate, add and subtract fractions with the same denominator (within one whole).
Use knowledge of equivalence to compare and order unit fractions and fractions with the same denominator, using the symbols =, > and <.

beats.say: A pizza is cut into four pieces. Are they all quarters?
Only if the pieces are equal. Equal is the word that does the work.
Here are two shapes. Each one is cut into four pieces.
Look at this one. Every piece is exactly the same size.
So these four pieces really are quarters.
Now the other one. This piece is bigger than the rest.
Four pieces is not enough. Fractions must be equal parts.
This bar is cut into five equal pieces, so each one is a fifth.
Colour them in, one at a time. Watch the top number climb.
Five fifths is not nearly one whole. It is one whole.
A square cut down the middle. A square cut corner to corner. A circle cut across.

at.middle: A square cut down the middle

beats.say: Every one of them is a half. The shape does not decide the fraction.
A fraction can be part of a group, not just part of a shape.

at.group: A fraction can be part of a group

beats.say: Zara has twelve beads. She wants a quarter of them.
The bottom number says four, so share them into four equal piles.
Three beads in every pile. Take one pile, and that is three.
The bottom number tells you how many piles, not how many to take.
The line in a fraction is a dividing line.
Three quarters means three shared between four.
Amina has twenty shillings. What is three quarters of that?
Divide by the bottom number first. Twenty shared into four is five.
Then multiply by the top. Three fives are fifteen shillings.
Two fifths, and one more fifth. Count the pieces: three fifths.
The bottom number never changes. It is never three tenths.
Now look at one half, and five tenths under it.
Both bars are coloured exactly the same amount.
Bigger numbers do not make a bigger fraction.
When the bottom numbers match, the pieces are the same size.
So three fifths is bigger than two fifths. More pieces wins.
But one quarter is bigger than one tenth. That sounds wrong.
Sharing between fewer people gives everybody a bigger piece.
A fraction is equal parts, and all of them make one whole.
You can take a fraction of a group, because the line means divide.
Two fractions can be worth the same, and you can compare them.
Now go and fold some paper strips, and see the equal parts.
